title: Types of Massage: The Main Styles Explained
excerpt: The main types of massage, what each feels like and who it suits, with a table to help you choose.
content_html:
There are dozens of massage styles, but most belong to a few families: oil massages with long, flowing strokes; firm massages for tight muscles; pressure and stretching without oil; very light massage for fluid; and treatments built around heat or a tool. This guide explains the main types, what each one feels like and who it suits, with a table at the end to help you choose.

Oil massages for relaxation

These are the classic spa massages: you lie on a massage bed under a towel, and the therapist uses oil so the hands glide in long strokes. They suit a first massage and anyone who mainly wants to unwind.

Swedish massage

The most widely known massage in Europe and North America. It uses five basic strokes: long gliding strokes (effleurage), kneading (petrissage), friction, tapping (tapotement) and vibration. The pressure is light to medium. It took shape in Europe in the 19th century and is the base that many other styles build on.

Balinese massage

Bali's traditional full-body oil massage. It adds skin rolling, acupressure and gentle stretches to the long strokes, and the pressure can be light or firm. Our guide What Is Balinese Massage? explains it in detail.

Aromatherapy massage

A gentle oil massage in which the oil is mixed with essential oils chosen for their scent, such as lavender or eucalyptus. The massage itself is usually close to a Swedish massage.

Lomi lomi

A Hawaiian massage with long, continuous strokes made with the forearms as well as the hands, often flowing over several parts of the body at once.

Abhyanga

The warm oil massage of Ayurveda, India's traditional medicine. Generous amounts of warm herbal oil are worked over the whole body, often including the head.

Firm massages for tight muscles

These styles work more slowly and more firmly on muscles that stay tight, and they usually focus on a few areas instead of the whole body.

Deep tissue massage

Slow, firm strokes with the forearms, knuckles and thumbs reach the deeper layers of muscle. It suits long-standing tightness in the back, neck and shoulders, and it can feel intense. See our Swedish vs deep tissue massage guide for how the two compare, or our deep tissue massage.

Sports massage

A firm massage focused on the muscles you train or play with, often with stretching. It is used before an event, after one, or as part of training. We offer a sports massage for surfers, runners and active travellers.

Trigger point therapy

Steady pressure on small, tender knots in a muscle, held until the tenderness eases. It is often part of a deep tissue or sports massage.

Pressure and stretching, without oil

In these styles you usually stay dressed in loose clothing, and the work comes from pressing and, in some, stretching.

Thai massage

Firm pressure with the palms, thumbs and elbows, combined with assisted, yoga-like stretches, on a mat or firm mattress. Our guide What Is Thai Massage? covers its history and what happens in a session.

Shiatsu

A Japanese massage whose name means "finger pressure". The therapist presses points along the body with the fingers, thumbs and palms, with gentle stretches and no oil. We offer shiatsu massage from 30 minutes.

Tui na

A Chinese therapeutic massage, part of traditional Chinese medicine, that uses pushing, kneading and grasping through the clothes.

Reflexology

Thumb and finger pressure on points of the feet (and sometimes the hands) that reflexology links to other parts of the body. Our foot reflexology chart shows the map, and we offer foot reflexology sessions too.

Light massage

Lymphatic drainage massage

A slow, very light massage that moves the skin in the direction lymph flows. Many people use it for puffy legs and ankles, for example after a long flight. Our guide to lymphatic drainage massage explains how it works.

Pregnancy massage

A gentle massage adapted for pregnancy, usually given lying on your side with pillows for support. Many therapists prefer to start after the first trimester, and you should check with your doctor or midwife first.

Massages with heat or tools

Hot stone massage

Smooth, heated basalt stones are used as massage tools and placed on the body, and the warmth helps muscles relax. Read about its benefits and what to expect.

Cupping

Cups create suction on the skin, usually on the back and shoulders, and leave round marks that fade over days. Our cupping therapy guide explains the marks and the evidence.

Candle massage

A massage candle, often made from shea butter or soy wax, melts at a low temperature into a warm oil that is poured onto the skin and massaged in. We offer it as a warm candle massage.

Short and seated massages

  • Head massage: the scalp, temples, neck and shoulders, often seated. The Indian version is known as champissage.

  • Foot massage: the soles, ankles and lower legs, a good choice after a day of walking.

  • Chair massage: a short, clothed massage of the back, neck and shoulders on a special chair, common at events and in offices.

Massage for two

A couples massage is not a technique but a setting: two people are massaged side by side in the same room, each by their own therapist, usually with the same style. Read more about our couples massage.

Which type of massage is best for you?

If you want to…

Try

Relax, or have your first massage

Swedish, Balinese or aromatherapy massage

Work on knots and long-standing tightness

Deep tissue or trigger point therapy

Recover from training or a surf trip

Sports massage

Stretch and loosen up, with no oil

Thai massage or shiatsu

Ease puffy legs after a flight

Lymphatic drainage massage

Feel warmth on tense muscles

Hot stone or candle massage

Rest tired feet

Foot massage or reflexology

Share the experience

A couples massage

Before your first massage

Tell the therapist about injuries, pregnancy, medical conditions and the pressure you like, and say straight away if anything feels uncomfortable. Our guides on what to wear to a massage and how often to get one answer the other common questions.

In short

For relaxation, choose an oil massage such as Swedish or Balinese. For tight muscles, choose deep tissue or sports massage. For stretching without oil, choose Thai or shiatsu, and for puffy legs, lymphatic drainage. Most of these are on our massage menu in Seminyak.

Frequently asked questions

What is the most common type of massage?

Swedish massage is the most common in Europe and North America. In Bali, it is Balinese massage, which is similar but adds acupressure and skin rolling.

Which type of massage is the most relaxing?

Slow oil massages with light to medium pressure, such as Swedish, Balinese or aromatherapy massage. Hot stone massage adds warmth, which many people find even more relaxing.

Which massage is best for back pain?

For everyday tightness, a deep tissue massage or a firm Balinese massage. Massage can ease back pain for a while, but see a doctor if pain lasts more than a few weeks or comes with numbness or weakness.

What is the difference between deep tissue and sports massage?

Both are firm. Deep tissue massage works slowly on long-standing tightness wherever it is, while a sports massage focuses on the muscles you use for your sport, often with stretching.

Which massages are done without oil?

Thai massage, shiatsu, tui na, reflexology and chair massage. You usually stay dressed in loose clothing.

Which massage is best for a first-timer?

A Swedish or Balinese massage, because the pressure is easy to adjust and nothing happens that will surprise you.
author: Spa Bali Moon
seo_title: Types of Massage: 20 Styles and How to Choose
seo_description: The main types of massage explained, from Swedish, Balinese and deep tissue to Thai, shiatsu, hot stone and cupping, with a table to help you choose.

title: Bali Belly: Causes, Prevention and What to Do
excerpt: What causes Bali belly, how to avoid it, what to do if you get it and when to see a doctor.
content_html:
Bali belly is the local name for travellers' diarrhoea: loose stools and stomach cramps, sometimes with nausea, vomiting or a mild fever, usually in the first week of a trip. It is caused by germs in food or water, and most cases clear up on their own within a few days. This guide explains what causes it, how to lower your risk, what to do if you get it and when to see a doctor.

What is Bali belly?

Bali belly is travellers' diarrhoea, the most common illness among people who travel. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that it affects 30% to 70% of travellers, depending on where they go and when.

The usual signs are:

  • three or more loose or watery stools in a day;

  • stomach cramps and an urgent need for the toilet;

  • nausea, and sometimes vomiting;

  • a mild fever or feeling generally unwell.

It usually lasts a few days, and most people are better within a week.

What causes Bali belly?

Most cases are caused by bacteria, especially a type of E. coli, in food or water that has been in contact with traces of faeces. Viruses such as norovirus cause many others, and parasites such as Giardia a few. Spicy food and a change of diet can upset the stomach, but they are not what causes Bali belly.

The usual sources are:

  • tap water, and drinks or ice made with it;

  • salads and raw vegetables washed in tap water;

  • raw or undercooked seafood, meat and eggs;

  • food that has sat at room temperature, such as at some buffets;

  • fruit that someone else has cut and left out;

  • hands that haven't been washed before eating.

How to avoid Bali belly

  1. Drink sealed bottled water or water from a filtered refill station, and don't drink tap water. Many people use bottled water to brush their teeth too.

  2. Be choosy about ice. In tourist areas, most restaurants and cafés buy ice made from purified water. If you aren't sure where the ice came from, skip it.

  3. Eat food that is cooked fresh and served hot. Busy places with a quick turnover are a good sign.

  4. Peel fruit yourself, and go easy on raw salads and raw seafood.

  5. Wash your hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet.

Probiotics are popular for prevention, but the evidence that they work is weak.

What to do if you get Bali belly

  • Drink plenty, in small sips if you feel sick. An oral rehydration solution (ORS) replaces the salts you lose. In Indonesia it is sold in sachets as oralit at every pharmacy (apotek).

  • Eat when you feel like it, starting with plain food such as rice, toast, bananas or clear soup.

  • Rest, and stay out of the heat, which makes you lose fluid faster.

  • Anti-diarrhoeal tablets such as loperamide can help adults when they need to travel or go out. Don't take them if you have blood in your stool or a high temperature, and don't give them to children under 12.

  • Antibiotics only help some cases. Take them only if a doctor prescribes them.

Avoid alcohol, coffee and very sugary drinks until you feel better, because they can make diarrhoea worse.

When to see a doctor

See a doctor straight away if you have:

  • blood or mucus in your stool;

  • a fever of 39°C (102°F) or higher;

  • vomiting that stops you keeping fluids down;

  • signs of dehydration: very little or dark urine, dizziness, a very dry mouth, or confusion;

  • severe stomach pain.

See one sooner, too, if you are pregnant, older, have a long-term condition such as diabetes or kidney disease, or if a young child is ill. Also see a doctor if you are no better after three days. Bali has international clinics in the main tourist areas, and many doctors visit hotels and villas.

Do you need an IV drip for Bali belly?

Usually not. If you can keep fluids down, an oral rehydration solution works well. A drip makes sense when vomiting stops you from drinking, and a doctor should check you first. Our guide IV drip therapy: before you book explains what a drip can and cannot do.

Getting back to your holiday

Give yourself a day or two of rest and plenty of fluids after the symptoms stop, and go easy on alcohol and rich food. Wait until you feel well before booking a massage: massage isn't a good idea while you have a fever or diarrhoea. When you are ready, a gentle Balinese massage in Seminyak is an easy way back into your holiday.

This guide gives general information and is not a substitute for medical advice.

Frequently asked questions

How long does Bali belly last?

Usually a few days. Most people are better within a week. See a doctor if you are no better after three days, or sooner if you have warning signs such as blood in your stool or a high fever.

Is Bali belly contagious?

It can be. The germs spread through food, water and unwashed hands, so wash your hands well and don't prepare food for others while you are ill.

Can you drink the tap water in Bali?

No. Drink sealed bottled water or filtered water, and many visitors brush their teeth with it too.

Is the ice safe in Bali?

In most restaurants and cafés in tourist areas, yes: they buy ice made from purified water. If you can't tell where the ice came from, skip it.

What should I eat with Bali belly?

Plain food in small amounts once you feel like eating, such as rice, toast, bananas, crackers and clear soup. Keep drinking an oral rehydration solution.

Does Coca-Cola help Bali belly?

Not really. Sugary fizzy drinks can make diarrhoea worse. An oral rehydration solution replaces fluid and salts much better.

Should I take antibiotics for Bali belly?

Only if a doctor prescribes them. Most cases get better without antibiotics, and they don't help when a virus is the cause.

title: Foot Reflexology Chart
excerpt: A foot reflexology chart with every zone explained, how to read it, and what reflexology can and can't do.
content_html:
A foot reflexology chart is a map of the soles of the feet that links each area to another part of the body: the toes to the head, the ball of the foot to the chest, the arch to the stomach and intestines, and the heel to the lower back and pelvis. Reflexologists use it to decide where to press. This guide shows the chart, explains how to read it, and says what reflexology can and can't do.

The foot reflexology chart

The chart shows the soles as if you were looking up at them through a glass floor: the left foot on the left, the right foot on the right, and the big toes on the inside. The body is laid over the feet with the head at the toes and the pelvis at the heels, and the right side of the body on the right foot. Most points appear on both feet; the chart labels each one once.

How to read a reflexology chart

Reflexology charts divide each foot with four lines across the sole, which split the body into five bands:

Part of the foot

Linked in reflexology to

Toes

Head, brain and sinuses; the base of the big toe to the neck

Base of the toes

Eyes (under the second and third toes) and ears (under the fourth and fifth)

Ball of the foot

Chest and lungs, the heart (mainly the left foot) and the shoulders (outer edge)

Upper arch

Liver and gallbladder (right foot), stomach, pancreas and spleen (mainly the left foot), and the kidneys

Lower arch

Small intestine, large intestine (colon) and bladder

Heel

Lower back, pelvis and the sciatic nerve

Inner edge, from big toe to heel

The spine: neck at the top, lower back at the bottom

The lines have names: the shoulder line at the base of the toes, the diaphragm line below the ball of the foot, the waist line across the middle of the arch, and the pelvic line where the heel begins. Charts differ in small details, but they all follow this layout.

Where foot reflexology comes from

Pressing and massaging the feet is an old practice in many cultures, including China and India. Modern reflexology started with "zone therapy", described by the American doctor William Fitzgerald in the 1910s, who divided the body into ten zones running from head to toe. In the 1930s the American physiotherapist Eunice Ingham turned his idea into the detailed foot maps used today.

What happens in a reflexology session

You sit back or lie down with your shoes and socks off, fully dressed. The therapist cleans and warms the feet, then works across each sole and along the sides with the thumbs and fingers, using small "thumb walking" movements and steady pressure on points from the chart. Most sessions last 30 to 60 minutes.

Some points feel tender, especially if you have been walking a lot. The pressure should feel firm but comfortable, so tell the therapist if it is too strong.

Does reflexology work?

There is no scientific evidence that pressing a point on the foot affects the organ the chart links it to, and reflexology can't diagnose or treat illness. If you have symptoms, see a doctor.

As a foot massage, though, it is pleasant and relaxing. Small studies have found that reflexology can ease anxiety and some kinds of pain for a while, much as other massage can. Most people simply find it soothing, especially after a long day on their feet.

How to try reflexology at home

  1. Sit comfortably and rest one foot on the opposite knee.

  2. Warm the foot by rubbing it between your hands for a minute.

  3. "Thumb walk" across the sole: bend and straighten the top joint of your thumb so it creeps forward in tiny steps, from the heel to the toes.

  4. Work along the inner edge of the foot, the spine line, from the heel up to the big toe.

  5. Press and circle any tender spot for 10 to 20 seconds, then move on.

  6. Squeeze and gently pull each toe, then repeat on the other foot.

Who should be careful

Reflexology is gentle and low risk. Skip it, or check with your doctor first, if you have a foot injury, an infection, broken skin, gout in the foot, a blood clot or poor circulation in the legs, or diabetes with numb feet. If you are pregnant, tell the therapist.

In short

A foot reflexology chart maps the body onto the soles: the head at the toes, the chest at the ball of the foot, the abdomen in the arch and the pelvis at the heel. Reflexology doesn't treat the organs on the chart, but it is a relaxing foot massage, especially after a day of walking. If you are in Bali, you can book foot reflexology in Seminyak at our spa or at your villa or hotel.

Frequently asked questions

What does the big toe relate to in reflexology?

The head and brain. The base of the big toe is linked to the neck, and its inner edge to the top of the spine.

Which part of the foot is linked to the kidneys?

The middle of the arch, on both feet, just above the waist line.

Which foot is the heart on in reflexology?

Mainly the left foot, on the ball of the foot towards the inner side.

What does it mean if a point on my foot hurts?

Usually that the area is tired or tight, often from walking or tight shoes. Reflexologists may read it as a sign about the linked organ, but there is no evidence for that.

Is reflexology the same as a foot massage?

Not quite. A foot massage relaxes the feet with general strokes and kneading. Reflexology follows the chart and uses thumb and finger pressure on specific points.

How often can you have reflexology?

As often as you like. It is gentle, so once or twice a week is fine.
author: Spa Bali Moon

seo_description: A foot reflexology chart with every zone explained: toes, ball, arch and heel, how to read it, where reflexology comes from and what it can and can't do.

title: Cupping Therapy: Benefits, Marks and What to Expect
excerpt: The types of cupping, what the research says, what the marks mean and what a session is like.
content_html:
Cupping therapy places cups on the skin, usually on the back and shoulders, and uses suction to lift the skin and the tissue beneath it. It leaves round marks that fade over a few days to two weeks. Many people find it eases tight muscles for a while, but the research is limited. This guide explains the types of cupping, what the marks mean, what a session is like and who should avoid it.

What is cupping therapy?

In cupping, the therapist creates suction inside a cup and places it on the skin, which is drawn up a little way into the cup. The cups stay in place for 5 to 10 minutes, or are glided over oiled skin. Cups can be made of glass, plastic, silicone or bamboo.

Cupping is old and found in many cultures. It is part of traditional Chinese medicine, and in the Middle East and the Muslim world wet cupping is known as hijama. It became widely known in 2016, when swimmers at the Rio Olympics, including Michael Phelps, competed with round purple marks on their shoulders.

Types of cupping

  • Dry cupping: suction only. The cups stay still on the skin for a few minutes.

  • Wet cupping (hijama): after dry cupping, the therapist makes tiny scratches in the skin and puts the cup back on to draw out a small amount of blood. It needs sterile, single-use blades and a trained practitioner.

  • Fire cupping: a flame briefly heats the air inside a glass cup, which creates suction as it cools on the skin.

  • Pump cupping: a small hand pump draws air out of the cup, so there is no flame and the suction is easy to adjust.

  • Gliding cupping: the cup is moved over oiled skin like a massage stroke, and it leaves lighter marks.

Cupping therapy benefits

Most research on cupping looks at pain. Reviews, summarised by the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, suggest cupping may ease neck and lower back pain for a short time. The studies are mostly small and of low quality, so it is hard to say how much of the effect comes from the cupping itself.

What people say they notice:

  • tight shoulders and back feel looser;

  • a warm, heavy, relaxed feeling in the area afterwards;

  • relief after training, surfing or long hours at a desk.

Cupping does not remove toxins, and it is not a treatment for illness.

What do cupping marks mean?

The round marks come from suction pulling blood out of tiny blood vessels under the skin, much like a bruise. They range from pink to dark purple and usually fade within a few days to two weeks.

In traditional Chinese medicine, practitioners read the colour as a sign of "stagnation" in the area. Medically, the colour mostly depends on how strong the suction was, how long the cup stayed on, and your skin. Darker marks do not mean more toxins. Marks are often darker where muscles are tight and the first time you have cupping, and lighter in later sessions.

What happens during a cupping session

  1. The therapist asks about your health, medicines and skin, then warms the back with a short massage and a little oil.

  2. Cups go on the back and shoulders, usually four to ten at a time, and stay for 5 to 10 minutes.

  3. The cups come off with a gentle release of the seal, and the area is massaged again.

Cupping feels like a firm pull or tightness, not a sharp pain. Tell the therapist if a cup feels too strong, and they can release some of the suction.

After cupping

  • Keep the area covered and warm for the rest of the day.

  • Keep strong sun off the marks for a day or two, as the skin can be sensitive.

  • Drink water and take it easy. Some people feel tired or a little light-headed afterwards.

  • After wet cupping, keep the small cuts clean and dry until they heal.

Who should avoid cupping

Skip cupping, or check with your doctor first, if you:

  • are pregnant;

  • have a bleeding disorder or anaemia, or take blood-thinning medicine;

  • have sunburn, a rash, broken skin, or an infection where the cups would go;

  • have diabetes, a heart condition or a pacemaker;

  • have a fever or feel unwell.

The usual side effects are the marks themselves, some soreness and, rarely, small blisters. Fire cupping can burn the skin, and wet cupping can lead to infection if the equipment isn't sterile.

In short

Cupping uses suction cups on the back and shoulders. It may ease muscle pain for a while, the evidence is limited, and the marks are harmless bruise-like spots that fade within two weeks. If you are in Bali, our cupping therapy in Seminyak uses solid cups and a small hand pump, with no flame, at our spa or at your villa or hotel.

Frequently asked questions

How long do cupping marks last?

Usually a few days to two weeks, depending on the suction, how long the cups stayed on and your skin.

Does cupping hurt?

It shouldn't. It feels like a strong pull on the skin. Tell the therapist if a cup feels too tight, and they can ease the suction.

What do dark cupping marks mean?

That more blood was drawn into the skin, often because of stronger or longer suction, or tight muscles. They are not a sign of toxins and fade like a bruise.

How often can you have cupping?

Wait until the marks have faded before cupping the same area again, which usually means one or two weeks.

What is the difference between dry and wet cupping?

Dry cupping uses suction only. Wet cupping adds tiny scratches in the skin so the cup draws out a little blood.

Can I swim or sunbathe after cupping?

Swimming is fine once any wet cupping cuts have closed. Keep strong sun off the marks for a day or two.
author: Spa Bali Moon

title: Swedish vs Deep Tissue Massage
excerpt: How Swedish and deep tissue massage differ in pressure, pace and purpose, and which one suits you.
content_html:
Swedish massage uses light to medium pressure and long, flowing strokes to relax the whole body. Deep tissue massage uses slow, firm pressure to work into the deeper layers of tight muscles, usually in a few problem areas. Choose Swedish to unwind and deep tissue for knots and long-standing tightness. This guide compares the two in detail.

What is Swedish massage?

Swedish massage is the classic Western oil massage, and the one most spas in Europe and North America mean by "a massage". It took shape in Europe in the 19th century and uses five basic strokes:

  • Effleurage: long, gliding strokes;

  • Petrissage: kneading and lifting the muscle;

  • Friction: small, firm circles;

  • Tapotement: light, rhythmic tapping;

  • Vibration: fine shaking of a muscle.

The pressure is light to medium, the pace is steady, and the therapist works over the whole body. Most people feel calm and sleepy afterwards.

What is deep tissue massage?

Deep tissue massage uses many of the same strokes, but much more slowly and firmly, to reach the deeper layers of muscle and the connective tissue around them. The therapist uses the forearms, knuckles, elbows and thumbs, waits for the muscle to soften, then goes a little deeper.

It usually focuses on a few areas, such as the upper back, neck, shoulders or lower back, instead of covering the whole body evenly. It feels intense, and some people are sore for a day or two afterwards.

Swedish vs deep tissue: the main differences

Swedish massage

Deep tissue massage

Pressure

Light to medium

Firm

Pace

Steady and flowing

Slow

Main goal

Relaxation

Loosening long-standing tightness

Areas

Whole body

A few problem areas

Therapist uses

Hands, mostly palms

Forearms, knuckles, elbows and thumbs

How it feels

Soothing

Intense but bearable

Afterwards

Calm and sleepy

Looser, sometimes sore for a day or two

Which one should you choose?

Choose Swedish massage if:

  • you want to relax, de-stress or sleep better;

  • it is your first massage;

  • you don't like firm pressure;

  • you are tired after travel rather than sore.

Choose deep tissue massage if:

  • you have knots or tightness that keeps coming back;

  • your shoulders and neck are stiff from desk work;

  • you train, surf or do physical work;

  • light massages feel like they don't reach the problem.

If you are somewhere in between, ask for a medium-pressure massage with extra time on the tight areas. Most therapists can do both in one session.

Does deep tissue massage hurt?

It should feel intense but not painful. A good guide is 6 or 7 out of 10: strong, but you can breathe and relax into it. Sharp pain, numbness or tingling means the pressure is too strong or in the wrong place, so say so straight away.

Some people feel sore for a day or two afterwards, like after exercise. Drinking water, a warm shower and gentle movement help. Bruising is not normal; tell your therapist next time if it happens.

Who should be careful with deep tissue massage

Choose a gentle massage, or check with your doctor first, if you:

  • take blood-thinning medicine or have a bleeding disorder;

  • have or have had a blood clot;

  • have osteoporosis or a recent fracture;

  • have had surgery recently;

  • are pregnant.

The US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health notes that the rare serious injuries linked to massage mostly involve vigorous styles such as deep tissue massage.

Where Balinese and sports massage fit

Balinese massage sits between the two: an oil massage like Swedish, but with acupressure and skin rolling, at a pressure you choose. Sports massage is firm like deep tissue but focuses on the muscles you use for your sport, often with stretching. Our guide to types of massage covers these and more.

In short

Swedish massage is a relaxing full-body massage with light to medium pressure. Deep tissue massage is slower and firmer, for tight, overworked muscles. We don't list a Swedish massage in Bali; the closest is our Balinese massage. For firm work, book a deep tissue massage in Seminyak, at our spa or at your villa or hotel.

Frequently asked questions

Is Swedish or deep tissue massage better for back pain?

For tight, sore muscles, deep tissue massage usually helps more. For back pain that comes with stress, a Swedish massage may be enough. See a doctor if back pain lasts more than a few weeks.

Can I ask for medium pressure?

Yes. Pressure is a scale, not two settings. Tell the therapist what you like at the start, and adjust it during the massage.

How sore will I be after a deep tissue massage?

Some people feel nothing; others are sore for a day or two, like after a workout. It should never feel like an injury.

Is deep tissue the same as sports massage?

No. Both are firm, but sports massage focuses on the muscles you use for your sport, often with stretching. Deep tissue works on tightness wherever it is.

How often should I get a deep tissue massage?

Give your muscles a few days between sessions. For ongoing tightness, once a week or every two weeks is common.

What should I do after a deep tissue massage?

Drink water, move gently and take a warm shower. Avoid hard exercise for the rest of the day.
author: Spa Bali Moon
seo_title: Swedish vs Deep Tissue Massage: Differences and Which to Choose

title: Hot Stone Massage: Benefits and What to Expect
excerpt: How a hot stone massage works, its benefits, what happens in a session and who should skip it.
content_html:
A hot stone massage is an oil massage in which smooth, heated stones are used as massage tools and placed on the body. The warmth relaxes muscles, so the therapist can work deeper with less pressure, and most people find it one of the most soothing massages there is. This guide explains how it works, its benefits, what a session is like and who should skip it.

What is a hot stone massage?

In a hot stone massage, the therapist heats smooth stones in water, oils your skin and uses the stones in two ways: held in the hand to glide along the muscles like a warm palm, and placed on the body, for example along the back or in the palms, while other areas are massaged.

The stones are usually basalt, a dark volcanic rock that holds heat well and is worn smooth by rivers or the sea. Some therapists also use cool marble stones to finish, which feels refreshing.

Heated stones have been used in many cultures. The modern spa version took shape in the United States in the 1990s and spread around the world.

Hot stone massage benefits

Research on hot stone massage specifically is limited, so most of what we know comes from studies of massage and heat in general:

  • Relaxation: warmth and slow strokes calm you down, and massage in general can ease stress and anxiety for a while.

  • Looser muscles: heat helps muscles relax, so tight areas often soften faster than with hands alone.

  • Deeper work, less pressure: because warm muscles give way more easily, the therapist can reach deeper without pressing as hard. That suits people who want deep work but find deep tissue massage too intense.

  • Comfort when you feel cold: after a long, air-conditioned flight or a rainy day, the warmth alone feels good.

What happens during a hot stone massage

  1. The therapist asks about your health and how much warmth and pressure you like.

  2. The stones are heated in water, and the therapist tests each one on their own skin before it touches yours.

  3. Your skin is oiled, then the therapist massages with the stones in long strokes, starting with the back.

  4. Warm stones may rest along the spine, on the palms or between the toes while other areas are worked.

  5. The massage ends with hands only, or with cool stones.

The stones should feel very warm but never too hot. Say straight away if one feels uncomfortable; the therapist will move it or let it cool.

Hot stone vs other massages

Hot stone

Deep tissue

Balinese

Pressure

Medium, feels deep

Firm

Light to firm

Warmth

Yes, from the stones

No

Best for

Deep relaxation, tight but tender muscles

Relaxing, a first massage

Who should skip a hot stone massage

Choose a massage without heat, or check with your doctor first, if you:

  • are pregnant;

  • have diabetes or nerve damage that reduces feeling in your skin, as you may not notice if a stone is too hot;

  • have high blood pressure or a heart condition;

  • have varicose veins, a blood clot or a bleeding disorder, or take blood-thinning medicine;

  • have sunburn, a rash, broken skin or a recent injury with swelling.

In Bali, sunburn is the most common reason to wait. Heat on sunburnt skin is painful, so choose a cooling treatment first, such as our sunburn treatment in Seminyak.

In short

A hot stone massage combines an oil massage with warm basalt stones. The heat relaxes muscles, so you get a deep-feeling massage without heavy pressure. Skip it if you are pregnant, sunburnt or have reduced feeling in your skin. If you are in Bali, you can book a hot stone massage in Seminyak at our spa or at your villa or hotel.

Frequently asked questions

Does a hot stone massage burn?

It shouldn't. The therapist tests each stone before using it and keeps it moving. Tell them straight away if a stone feels too hot.

What stones are used in a hot stone massage?

Usually basalt, a smooth volcanic rock that holds heat well. Some therapists also use cool marble stones.

Is hot stone massage good for back pain?

It can ease tight back muscles for a while, and the warmth helps them relax. See a doctor for back pain that lasts more than a few weeks.

Can I have a hot stone massage when pregnant?

Most spas don't offer hot stone massage during pregnancy, because of the heat. A gentle pregnancy massage is a better choice, with your doctor's or midwife's OK.

Is hot stone massage better than deep tissue?

Neither is better. Hot stone massage feels deep with less pressure and is more relaxing; deep tissue massage works more firmly on stubborn knots.

How long does a hot stone massage last?

Usually 60 to 90 minutes. Ours are 1 hour, 1.5 hours or 2 hours.

title: What to Wear to a Massage
excerpt: What to wear for an oil massage, a Thai massage or a massage at your villa, and the questions people feel shy asking.
content_html:
For an oil massage, you undress to your comfort level, usually down to your underwear, and stay covered by a towel or sheet, with only the area being massaged uncovered. For Thai massage, shiatsu and reflexology, you stay dressed in loose clothing. To get to the spa, wear something comfortable that is easy to take off and put back on.

What to wear for an oil massage

Swedish, Balinese, deep tissue, hot stone and aromatherapy massages all use oil, so the therapist needs to reach your skin. You undress in private (the therapist leaves the room or waits outside) and lie under a towel or sheet.

  • Underwear: most people keep it on. Many spas give you disposable briefs so your own don't get oily.

  • Bra: for a back massage, most women take it off, because the straps are in the way. You can keep it on if you prefer, and the therapist will work around it.

  • Fully undressed: fine at most spas. You are covered at all times, and only the part being massaged is uncovered, then covered again. This is called draping.

You are never expected to undress more than you are comfortable with. Tell the therapist your preference; it changes nothing about the massage.

What to wear for a massage without oil

For Thai massage, shiatsu, reflexology and chair massage, you stay dressed. Wear loose, stretchy clothing such as a T-shirt and yoga trousers or shorts, or change into the clothes the spa gives you. Avoid jeans, belts and anything tight, because Thai massage includes stretches.

For a foot massage or reflexology, shorts or trousers that roll up to the knee are ideal.

What to wear to the spa

  • Loose, comfortable clothes that are easy to take off and put back on.

  • Slip-on shoes or sandals.

  • Little or no jewellery; you will take it off anyway.

  • A hair tie if you have long hair.

  • For a facial, come without make-up if you can, or the therapist will remove it.

After an oil massage, some oil stays on your skin, so avoid wearing silk or anything you don't want marked.

A massage at your villa or hotel

The same rules apply when a therapist comes to you. They bring fresh linen, towels and oils, and step outside while you change. Have a robe or sarong ready, and keep the room cool but not cold.

Other common questions

  • Shaving: not needed. Therapists don't notice or mind.

  • Your period: a massage is fine. Wear a tampon or menstrual cup, or keep your underwear on, and tell the therapist if you'd like them to avoid your stomach.

  • Feeling shy: completely normal. Keep on what you like, and say if anything makes you uncomfortable.

  • Contact lenses and glasses: lenses are fine, but take glasses off before you lie face down.

In short

For an oil massage, keep your underwear on or not, as you prefer: you stay covered by a towel either way. For Thai massage and shiatsu, wear loose clothes you can stretch in. Our guide to types of massage shows which styles use oil, and if you'd rather stay at your villa, our home service massage in Seminyak brings the therapist to you.

Frequently asked questions

Do you have to take your clothes off for a massage?

Only for an oil massage, and only as much as you like. Thai massage, shiatsu and reflexology are done fully clothed.

Should I wear underwear during a massage?

It's up to you. Most people do, and many spas give you disposable briefs. You stay covered by a towel either way.

What should I wear for a Thai massage?

Loose, stretchy clothing such as a T-shirt and yoga trousers, or the clothes the spa provides. No oil is used.

Do I need to shave before a massage?

No. It makes no difference to the massage, and therapists don't mind.

Can I get a massage on my period?

Yes. Wear a tampon or menstrual cup, or keep your underwear on, and tell the therapist if you'd like them to avoid your stomach.

What should I wear after a massage?

Loose clothes you don't mind getting a little oily, and sandals. Many people go straight to bed or the pool.

title: How Often Should You Get a Massage?
excerpt: How often to get a massage for relaxation, back pain, sport or pregnancy, and how many to book on holiday.
content_html:
There is no single right answer, but common rhythms are: once a month to relax and manage stress; every week or two for ongoing tightness or back pain, then less often as it improves; and weekly during heavy training. On holiday, two or three massages spread over a week is plenty. The benefits of massage fade over days, so regular sessions are what keep them going.

How often, by goal

Your goal

A common rhythm

Relaxation and stress

Every 2 to 4 weeks

Ongoing tightness, neck or back pain

Every 1 to 2 weeks at first, then every 3 to 4 weeks

Sports training

Weekly, or after hard sessions and events

Puffy legs (lymphatic drainage)

A short series, such as 2 or 3 sessions in a week

Pregnancy

Every 2 to 4 weeks, with your doctor's or midwife's OK

A holiday

2 or 3 in a week, with a day between firm massages

These are common starting points, not rules. Your budget, your time and how your body responds matter more.

Why regular massage works better than the odd one

Research summarised by the US National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health finds that the benefits of massage, such as less pain or less stress, are real but short-lived. A single massage feels great for a day or two; a regular rhythm keeps tight muscles from building back up as quickly.

For long-standing tightness, the first few sessions do the most work. Once the muscles stay looser between massages, you can space them out.

Can you get a massage every day?

A gentle massage every day is safe for most people. Firm massages are different: after a deep tissue or sports massage, give your muscles a day or two to recover before the next one, especially if you feel sore.

Signs you are overdoing it:

  • soreness that lasts more than two days;

  • bruising;

  • feeling worn out instead of relaxed.

How often on holiday

A week away is a good time to try a few styles, especially in Bali, where massage is part of daily life. A rhythm that works for many visitors:

  • Arrival day: something gentle, such as a lymphatic drainage or Balinese massage, to ease the flight. Our jet lag guide explains why.

  • Mid-week: something firmer, such as a deep tissue, sports or Thai massage, if surfing, hiking or sunbeds have left you stiff.

  • Before you fly home: a relaxing massage, or a foot massage after days of walking.

Leave a day between firm massages, and skip massage on sunburnt skin.

Who should check first

If you are pregnant, have a medical condition, take blood-thinning medicine or are recovering from an injury or surgery, ask your doctor how often massage is right for you. Tell the therapist at every visit.

In short

Once a month is a good rhythm for relaxation, every week or two for ongoing tightness, and weekly for athletes in training. On holiday, two or three massages in a week, with rest days between firm ones, is plenty. Our guide to types of massage helps you choose a style, and our massage menu in Seminyak lists every treatment and price.

Frequently asked questions

Is once a month enough?

For relaxation and general wellbeing, yes. For ongoing pain or tightness, more often at first usually works better.

How often should you get a massage for back pain?

Every week or two for the first few sessions, then less often as it improves. See a doctor if back pain lasts more than a few weeks or comes with numbness or weakness.

How long should you wait between deep tissue massages?

At least a few days, and longer if you are still sore. Once a week or every two weeks is common.

Is it bad to get a massage every day?

A gentle daily massage is fine for most people. Daily firm massages don't give muscles time to recover.

How many massages should I get on a week's holiday?

Two or three is plenty for most people, with a day between firm ones. Gentle massages such as Balinese or foot massage can be more frequent.

Does massage work better if you get it regularly?

Yes. The effects of a single massage fade within days, so a regular rhythm keeps muscles looser and stress lower.
